title: Design Patterns in C++
subtitle: Dr. Charles Dorner
description: Learn the design patterns through concrete problems, working C++, UML, and explained design choices. Use the chapter map to follow the lesson.
provenance: Study companion to Design Patterns in C++ by Dr. Charles Dorner. Lessons retain the supplied editable textbook’s chapter sections, example contracts, traces, focused explanations, exercises, lab instructions, and answers. Flashcards use those chapter explanations. Multiple-choice scenarios are original teaching questions. UML views render the supplied diagram definitions and exact focused source excerpts. This is a study companion, with the full runnable source in the C++ view and download package.

chapters.title: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system

glossary.definition: A virtual creation operation called by a creator’s inherited workflow, with concrete creation supplied by derived creators.
An object created for another operation to use.
A function that selects and constructs a product without requiring an overridable creation hook in a creator hierarchy.
An interface for creating the different product roles in one compatible family.
Writing a value and then reading it back to verify that its meaning is preserved.
Skipping the remaining part of a logical expression when the result is already decided.
An object that collects construction choices in steps and produces a completed product.
A reusable recipe that calls builder steps in a chosen sequence.
An independent value representing data at one point in time.
A C++ declaration granting a named class or function access to private and protected members.
A pattern in which an existing object creates a new object by copying its own state through a common operation.
Losing the derived part when a derived object is copied into a base value.
A copy that duplicates owned contents to the independence depth required by the application.
A copy that duplicates handles while retaining some shared underlying objects.
A design that controls access to one instance through a shared accessor.
A synchronization object used to allow one participating thread at a time into a protected region.
Code that accesses shared state while holding the required lock.
Unsynchronized conflicting accesses to memory by different threads, with at least one write; in C++ this causes undefined behavior.
Supplying an object a component needs through an explicit parameter or constructor instead of locating it globally.
A boundary object that translates an existing service into a contract another caller needs.
The existing service whose interface or meaning must be translated.
An adapter implemented by inheriting from a target interface and a legacy class.
The agreement about what physical unit a number represents.
A connection that lets a high-level operation and its implementation vary independently.
One independent kind of change, such as report meaning or output format.
The set of every pairing from two sets of choices.
A design in which leaves and containers support the same useful operation over a tree.
A tree node with no children.
Solving a problem by calling the same operation on smaller parts until a stopping case is reached.
Having no path that leads back to an earlier node.
An object that adds behavior around another object while keeping the same interface.
Describes operations whose result can change when their order is swapped.
Describes an operation whose repeated application has the same effect as applying it once.
A simpler public operation or interface over a related set of subsystem operations.
A rule a caller must establish before invoking an operation.
A small input unit, such as one whitespace-separated number.
A range that includes both stated endpoints.
A design that shares repeated state while keeping per-use state separate.
State that belongs to the shared object identity and can be reused across contexts.
State that belongs to one use of a shared object.
Reusing one stored object for repeated requests with an equal identity key.
Not changing after construction.
A substitute service object that controls access, location, or lifecycle while keeping the service interface.
Creating an object only when it is first needed.
A request answered from an already stored result.
Declaring a remembered result unusable so a later request must fetch again.
Remembered data that is no longer known to match the current source.
A callable that decides whether it is responsible for a request.
Ordered handlers with an explicit rule for passing or stopping requests.
A value wrapper that may contain one value or no value.
Stages that may each contribute work before a later stage runs.
An object that stores a request and provides an operation to perform it.
The object whose real state or service a command uses.
The point after which an operation is recorded as successfully applied.
A later action intended to offset an effect that cannot literally be undone.
An object that represents a position and a way to traverse a collection.
A valid traversal position after the last element, with no element to read.
An event that ends the permission to use an existing cursor or reference.
A value used to distinguish one collection version from another.
An object that owns rules for how other components work together.
A function call made back to code supplied or represented by another object.
A state change that deliberately sends no new change event.
A chain of events that returns to its starting point and may repeat.
A saved record of object state whose details are controlled by the state owner.
The object that creates and interprets its own snapshots.
An object that keeps snapshots without managing their internal representation.
The set of state restored together by one snapshot.
A listener registered to receive notifications about an event or change.
A non-owning observer of an object managed by shared ownership.
Entering an operation again before a previous call to it has finished.
A policy that stops notifying remaining listeners when a callback fails.
A current mode whose rules affect an object behavior.
A permitted change from one state to another in response to an event.
The object that owns current state and delegates state-dependent work.
A next-state value prepared before the context commits a change.
A replaceable object or callable that supplies one way to perform a task.
The object that keeps stable work and calls a selected strategy.
A rule that must already hold when an operation begins.
A base-class operation that fixes a sequence while letting derived classes replace selected steps.
An optional extension point with a useful default or an empty default action.
A rule that must be true when an operation successfully returns.
A derived declaration prevents ordinary lookup from finding a same-named base declaration; it is not necessarily an override.
An operation object with a separate entry point for each supported element type.
The compiler choosing a same-name function from its parameter types.
Selecting behavior using both the actual element kind and actual operation kind.
A design that names all allowed element alternatives in one known interface or value type.
The operation that makes a fully prepared change visible as the new accepted state.
For the stated objects and ordinary exception flow, a failed operation leaves their observable state unchanged.
A value converted into the one representation the internal program agrees to use.
The decision stored when data is admitted, preserved even if later policy changes.
A fixed set of named states with explicit rules for permitted changes between them.
A check that old required behavior still works after a change.
